title: Recording Audio Tricks
intro: Recording is the one part of the process you cannot fix later. These tricks are about getting a clean, usable, well‑organised take the first time, and never losing a good performance to a technical mistake.

tips.t: Check your input with the channel strip's meter, not your ears
tips.d: Aim for peaks around −12 dBFS with your loudest phrase. Recording hot is a habit from tape and it buys you nothing in 24‑bit.

tips.t: Drop the buffer to 64 samples for tracking
tips.d: Round‑trip latency below about 10 ms is the point where a performer stops noticing it. Do this before the singer walks in, not while they wait.

tips.t: Turn on Low Latency Mode instead of disabling plugins one by one
tips.d: It bypasses only the plugins that actually cause delay, keeping your monitoring chain intact.

tips.t: Count-in and pre-roll are either/or — pick the right one
tips.d: They are exclusive options in the recording settings, not two dials you stack. Count-in gives the performer the tempo from silence; pre-roll rolls the actual track into the punch. For punch-ins, choose pre-roll.

tips.t: Name the track before you record, always
tips.d: Logic names audio files after the track. “Audio 3#12.wav” three months later is a file you will never open again.
⌥‑click a record enable button to arm every track, or select several track headers and hit the record enable on one.
Turn on cycle and let the performer keep going. Every pass stacks into a take folder, ready to be comped. Never stop between takes.

tips.t: Punch in on the fly with R
tips.d: With Quick Punch‑In enabled, hitting R during playback drops you into record with the audio before the punch preserved.

Enable Autopunch and drag the punch range in the ruler — Logic records only inside that range no matter when you start playback. If you cannot see the Autopunch button, add it via Customize Control Bar.

tips.t: ⌘. discards the take you just recorded
tips.d: Stop and delete in one keystroke, when you know instantly that it was not the one.

tips.t: Watch the take folder count, not the waveform
tips.d: The take folder header shows how many passes you have. If the performer is on take 14 and getting worse, it is time to stop and move on.

tips.t: Build a dedicated headphone mix on a bus
tips.d: Send every track to a second output bus and give the performer more of themselves and more reverb than you would ever put in the mix. Comfort produces better takes than accuracy does.

tips.t: Add reverb to the monitoring only, not the recording
tips.d: Put the reverb on the headphone bus, not the input channel. The singer hears the polish; the file stays dry.

tips.t: Use Input Monitoring rather than record enable to rehearse
tips.d: The I button lets you hear the input without arming anything, so you can set levels and rehearse with zero risk of recording over something.

tips.t: Turn off software monitoring if you hear yourself twice
tips.d: The doubling is your interface's direct monitoring fighting Logic's. Pick one.

tips.t: Give the performer a click they can feel
tips.d: Swap the metronome sound, add a bar accent, or better, program a simple drum loop. A musical reference beats a woodblock every time.
